summary: All six depth packets are visibly used; none was skipped. The losses are of a single type: developed quantitative mechanisms compressed to a bare mention, or two-sided findings reported on one side only. Highest-value gaps: the App-Store margin provenance chain, the court-found 70%-gaming composition anchor, the EU sub-3% alternative-marketplace adoption that bounds erosion speed, the bull half of the Lam & Shankar loyalty mechanism, the supercycle-hangover decay trend, and the appellate posture fact that neither party attacks payment continuation on the merits.

findings.location: Section 1.2, paragraph 'App-Store-Kommissionen: nur Anbieterschaetzungen' (~line 17), sentence 'Als belegte Margenuntergrenze dient die Services-Bruttomarge von 75,4 % [1]; die Obergrenze von 85 % ist eine Annahme, hoehere kursierende Werte sind weder gerichtlich festgestellt noch Bruttomargen.'
findings.issue: The draft dismisses the circulating ~78%/~90% App Store margin figures in one subordinate clause, discarding the entire provenance chain the depth investigator built. That correction is the note's most load-bearing margin finding and it feeds the commission gross-profit line in Table 1.3 - i.e. it is load-bearing for the headline 19,7-28,3 % answer.
findings.evidence: interim-report-appstore-commission-magnitude-margin-and-scotus-reversal, 'What the new sources say' + 'Evidence synthesis / On margin': the 78%/79.6% figures come from Ned Barnes, an Epic Games damages EXPERT WITNESS, not a court finding; they are for 2018-2019 (seven years stale); Apple disputed them at trial; the 2021 Findings of Fact adopt no percentage ('I searched the full body for "78%", "profit margin" values, "Barnes", and "operating income" - none of the specific percentages appear'); the court's language is qualitative ('extraordinarily high', 'excessive', 'supracompetitive operating margins'); and the metric class is OPERATING margin, not gross margin. The note states: 'Do NOT use ~90% for anything; no source in this corpus supports it at any level of the analysis.' Services gross margin: 70.8% (FY23) / 73.9% (FY24) / 75.4% (FY25), from $60,345M / $71,050M / $82,314M over $85,200M / $96,169M / $109,158M.
findings.recommendation: Expand to two or three sentences: name Barnes as Epic's retained damages expert, the 2018-19 vintage, Apple's dispute, the court's refusal to certify any number (only 'supracompetitive operating margins'), and the operating-vs-gross metric-class error that makes the figure non-substitutable for the gross margin the decomposition needs. Add the FY2023-FY2025 Services gross-margin series with underlying dollars so the 75,4 % floor is visibly computed. Keep the note's flag that bridging Barnes's operating margin to a gross-margin equivalent is inference, not evidence.

findings.location: Section 4.3, closing paragraph (~line 169), sentence 'CFO Parekh nannte Mobile-Gaming-Schwaeche, Geschaeftsmodellaenderungen „in certain countries“ und das US-Urteil, ohne sie zu gewichten [11].'
findings.issue: The draft treats Parekh's three-cause attribution as an unweighted evasion and moves on, omitting the one judicially-found composition anchor that lets the reader weight it - and that anchor complicates the draft's own commitment that the erosion is court-driven. If gaming is ~70% of App Store revenue, 'mobile gaming softness' is a first-order non-litigation driver, not a deflection.
findings.evidence: interim-report-appstore-commission-magnitude-margin-and-scotus-reversal: the 2021 Findings of Fact state 'gaming apps account for approximately 70% of all App Store revenues', generated by 'less than 10% of all App Store consumers', on the standard 70/30 split - described in the note as 'one hard, judicially-found anchor that no vendor estimate can contradict', in contrast to every dollar figure in the corpus, which traces to Appfigures/Sensor Tower. The note lists as an open question that the split of the 2026 Services deceleration between US litigation, EU/other-country model changes and gaming softness 'is not quantified anywhere, including by Apple itself'.
findings.recommendation: Insert the 70%-of-revenue-from-under-10%-of-consumers court finding where Parekh's attribution is discussed and use it to qualify the erosion verdict: a base that concentrated in gaming means the litigation-specific drag cannot be read off the headline deceleration - which strengthens the draft's own point that the decisive number (the remand rate) does not yet exist. Also reference it at the 30-60 % Abschlag in Section 2.2 as an explicit uncertainty on that discount.

findings.location: Section 4.3 / Section 6.3 / Section 7.1 - wherever the durability and speed of commission erosion is committed (lines 169, 239, 255)
findings.issue: The draft never gives the number that bounds the SPEED of commission erosion, although it commits to a 30-60 % discount on that stream. The depth note names this figure as the load-bearing boundary condition on its own erosion verdict, and Section 7.1 treats the DMA natural experiment only at browser level while this is the app-distribution-level result.
findings.evidence: interim-report-appstore-commission-magnitude-margin-and-scotus-reversal, 'Committed position' and 'Boundary conditions': 'The offsetting force - genuinely low real-world uptake of alternative payment/marketplace options even where legally permitted (EU adoption <3% since March 2024, per the corpus's own contradiction graph) - bounds the SPEED of erosion but does not reverse its DIRECTION'; and 'most subscription IAP still flows through Apple's own checkout because consumer switching friction remains high - EU's <3% alternative-marketplace adoption is the load-bearing data point here'.
findings.recommendation: Add the sub-3 % EU alternative-marketplace adoption since March 2024 as the explicit speed bound, in the same place the draft argues the In-App-Checkout survives (Section 1.4 'Zweitens' and Section 4.3), then state the direction/speed split: direction durable, speed bounded - which is precisely what justifies a 30-60 % discount rather than a larger one and gives the bull case its strongest concrete counter.

findings.location: Section 7.1, paragraph 'Die bewertungsrelevante Einschraenkung' (~line 257), sentence citing Lam und Shankar (Koeffizient 0,61 -> 0,31) [78]
findings.issue: The draft uses only the bearish half of a two-result mechanism. The same study's second supported hypothesis runs the other way and is the mechanism that partly protects Apple across an interface shift; omitting it makes the paragraph one-sided and under-specifies a paper the draft leans on hard.
findings.evidence: interim-report-lockin-durability-preference-vs-ai-interface: H4 (supported, chi2(1)=7.17, p<.01) perceived value's effect on loyalty falls from .61 (existing generation) to .31 (new). H5 (supported, chi2(1)=10.13, p<.01) perceived benevolence/trust becomes a stronger POSITIVE driver for the new generation (coefficient .18) versus negative/non-driving for the existing one (-.18), because 'as uncertainty increases in the new generation, benevolence becomes salient in reducing consumers' vulnerability'. The note's applied reading: the 60,8 % of SellCell respondents citing 'prefer Apple' map to the transferable trust construct and are 'on firmer ground across an interface shift', but even that component 'flips sign and changes meaning' rather than persisting unchanged. Design: SEM, n=514, Singapore, ages 18-35, 2.5G->3G - a SMALLER paradigm shift than phone-to-AI-interface, so analogy not direct test.
findings.recommendation: Add H5 with coefficients and significance alongside H4, state the two-sided applied reading (value-based preference roughly halves; brand-trust transfers and becomes more important under uncertainty but changes functional form), and carry the note's scope caveat about the 2.5G->3G analogue. This strengthens the draft's Festlegung by explaining why hardware loyalty survives while interface-dependent rents do not.

findings.location: Section 7.3, paragraph after the static table (~line 276), sentence 'Eine Delle von -4 % bis -6 % entspricht der iPhone-X-Delle ... die iPhone-6-Delle (-12,8 %/-14,6 %) waere es nicht [85].'
findings.issue: The draft takes four numbers from a fully worked decay table but drops the table's actual finding - that each successive hangover has been progressively milder, with a named mechanism. That trend is the bull-side answer to research question 7 (is the required Services CAGR historically plausible?), and the draft currently answers only the bear half.
findings.evidence: interim-report-hardware-regime-and-required-services-cagr, decay table: iPhone 6 (peak FQ1 FY2015 +29.5%) -> Q+5/Q+6 of -12.8%/-14.6%, producing Apple's first-ever revenue-decline fiscal year FY2016; iPhone X (peak +12.7%) -> -4.5%/-5.1%, recovering to flat-to-positive by Q+6; iPhone 12 (peak +21.4%) -> positive through Q+7 (+8.1%), turning negative only at Q+8 (-5.5%) under the Dec-2022 Zhengzhou supply-shock confound. The note's reading: 'Each successive supercycle's hangover has been progressively less severe. That pattern is consistent with ... a rising Services mix cushioning total-company growth even as the hardware component decays, exactly the mechanism the query's "required services CAGR" question is asking about.' Stated caveats: total-company revenue used as an iPhone proxy (no iPhone-segment quarterly data for FY2015/FY2018); iPhone-12 Q+1..Q+3 inflated by COVID base effects.
findings.recommendation: Develop into the three-cycle progression with the decay figures, state the milder-each-time pattern and the Services-mix cushioning mechanism as the strongest historical support for the draft's own 'bounded shock absorber' verdict, and carry both confounds. This cuts toward the bull case on hardware normalisation and also belongs in Section 8.2's fair bull statement.

findings.location: Section 4.1, paragraph '**Zeitplan.**' (~line 146), sentence 'Google legte am 16. Januar 2026 Berufung ein (D.C. Cir. Nr. 26-5023); die Anschlussberufungen von DOJ und Bundesstaaten wurden am 5. Februar 2026 konsolidiert [39, 40].'
findings.issue: The draft says Google appealed but never what Google appealed - and the answer is the strongest single support for the draft's own modal 'Status quo' weight of 45-55 %. Without it the weight reads as constructed when the docket actually supports it.
findings.evidence: interim-report-google-tac-magnitude-repricing-and-appellate-tail, 'The D.C. Circuit docket': 'Google is Appellant, challenging (per the docket's own characterization) the data-sharing/syndication remedies and the extension of remedies to GenAI companies - i.e., Google is NOT appealing the payment-continuation/annual-rebidding piece, because it won that piece.' Also: final judgment Dec. 5, 2025; per curiam scheduling order April 30, 2026, panel Walker, Childs, Garcia; Google opening brief filed 05/22/2026 (20,787 words); DOJ/states Response-and-Cross-Appeal brief filed 07/28/2026 (170 pages); Google reply due 09/29/2026; deferred appendix 10/13/2026; cross-appellants' final reply 10/29/2026; no oral argument date set as of the docket's Sept. 10, 2026 update.
findings.recommendation: State explicitly that neither side attacks payment continuation on the merits - Google appeals only the data-sharing/syndication and GenAI-extension pieces, DOJ/states only the procedural finding - and use that as the sourced basis for the 45-55 % status-quo weight in Table 4.2. Name the panel (Walker, Childs, Garcia) and the absence of an argument date as of 10 September 2026, since Fruehindikator 6 already asks the reader to watch for one.

findings.location: Section 2.4 (~line 72) and Section 4.1 (~line 146), where the DOJ/states cross-appeal is characterised as 'eng und prozedural'
findings.issue: The draft reads the cross-appeal as procedural but omits its sharpest evidentiary move, which is the best textual support in the corpus for the Cap branch the draft weights at 25-35 %. As written the cross-appeal looks like a technicality; the interim note shows it is a technicality carrying Mehta's own diagnosis inside it.
findings.evidence: interim-report-google-tac-magnitude-repricing-and-appellate-tail: question presented verbatim - 'Whether the district court erred by rejecting a payment ban without first determining whether a remedy lacking a payment ban would effectively redress Google's violations and restore competition' - and DOJ quoting Mehta against himself: '[d]ue to Google's massive financial advantage and its superior monetization... without a payment ban distributors will be incentivized to stick with Google because it can pay more, thus leaving in place the very forces that effectively have made the ecosystem exceptionally resistant to change' (JA(Rem.Op.127)). The note adds that Mehta's footnote-14 'ill-equipped to consider [now]' language on the 'unconditional revenue share' middle ground reads as 'a correctable defect, not obviously an outcome-determinative one'.
findings.recommendation: Add the question presented verbatim and the Mehta-quoted-against-himself passage (German plus English original per the output contract) in Section 4.1, and add the footnote-14 'unconditional revenue share' opening as sourced support for why the intermediate cap branch, not the ban branch, carries the second-largest weight. This is the depth packet's most quotable material and appears nowhere in the draft.

findings.location: Section 1.2, paragraph '**Google TAC: gerichtlich verankert, modelliert fortgeschrieben.**' (~line 15), sentence 'Alphabets offengelegte TAC stieg von FY2022 bis FY2025 um 6,6 % p. a. ... [4].'
findings.issue: The 6,6 % rate converts the only court-anchored number ($20B, 2022) into the report's largest exposure figure (~26 Mrd. $), yet is presented as a bare rate. The interim note derives it from disclosed line items and surfaces a distinction that bears directly on the draft's own base case: Alphabet's TAC DOLLARS grow while the TAC RATE on ad revenue compresses.
findings.evidence: interim-report-google-tac-magnitude-repricing-and-appellate-tail, 'Alphabet FY2022 and FY2025 10-Ks': 'The TAC rate was 22% in both 2021 and 2022' against Google advertising revenue of $224,473M implies total TAC ~$49.4B (2022); 'The TAC rate decreased from 20.7% to 20.3% from 2024 to 2025' against $294,691M implies ~$59.8B (2025), and ~$54.8B in 2024 at 20.7% of $264,590M - a 21.1% increase FY2022-FY2025 = 6.6%/yr CAGR, driven per the filing by 'growth in TAC paid to distribution partners' even as the rate compresses 'primarily due to a revenue mix shift from Google Network properties to Google Search & other properties'. The note records as an audited disclosure absence that neither filing breaks out the distribution-partner sub-total or Apple's share, and that Google Network/AdSense publisher payments are blended into the same reported TAC line.
findings.recommendation: Show the derivation in one sentence (TAC rate x Google ad revenue for 2022 and 2025, ~$49.4B -> ~$59.8B, hence 6.6 %/yr), name the rate-compresses-while-dollars-grow pattern, and state the blended-line limitation. This turns the report's largest single estimate from an assertion into an auditable calculation and pre-empts the objection that Alphabet-wide TAC growth is not Apple-specific.

findings.location: Section 1.2 / Table 1.3 TAC row / Section 4.5 Ereigniskalender - anywhere the TAC magnitude appears
findings.issue: The report's framing is 'which arrangements can a US court void', yet the TAC figure is worldwide throughout and never split geographically. The depth investigator addressed this explicitly; the draft drops both the rough bound and the audited absence.
findings.evidence: interim-report-google-tac-magnitude-repricing-and-appellate-tail: 'The court is explicit this is a worldwide, not U.S., figure, and that "Google undoubtedly pays Apple billions of dollars for domestic distribution" without stating how many'; 'A U.S.-only figure cannot be defended to the same standard: no source in the corpus discloses or estimates it... I flag $10B-$14B as an illustrative, low-confidence U.S.-only band, not a defended estimate at the same confidence tier as the worldwide range - this should be presented in the report as an audited absence with a rough bound, not a point figure.'
findings.recommendation: Add one sentence noting the $23-29B run-rate is worldwide, that the court declined to state the US-only figure, and that an illustrative low-confidence band of roughly $10-14B is the most that can be said - labelled as such, not carried into any table. This matters because a US remedy reaches only the US slice, which caps the realistic downside of the C branch below what the draft's 'TAC-Wert ~0' row implies.

findings.location: Section 3.2 'Passive Flows: Exposition ist nicht Elastizitaet' (~line 97), and the sentence 'Eine Apple-spezifische Zahl gibt die Literatur nicht her, und keine wird hier behauptet.'
findings.issue: The exposure-vs-elasticity framing is right but three developed mechanisms are compressed to single clauses, and an audited absence is asserted without stating what was searched - which this run's deep-inference directive specifically requires.
findings.evidence: interim-report-passive-flow-apple-specific-magnitude: (1) KRY decomposition - aggregate institutional active share fell 38.9%->32.8% (6.1pp) over 2007Q4-2016Q4, of which -4.8pp is capital FLOWING active-to-passive versus only -1.3pp from strategy change, i.e. the flow channel is ~3.7x the behavioural one, producing the 14% repricing of the largest 90% of US firms. (2) Bouchaud - M is 'of order unity', ~1 at a monthly horizon (T_m ~ 20 trading days), derived from the square-root impact law I(Q,T) ~ Y * sigma_T * sqrt(Q/V_T) with Y~0.5 for US stocks; this is the sourced mechanism behind the below-average-multiplier claim. (3) Banafti & Lee - in the GIV framework ownership concentration (Herfindahl of unit sizes) governs the estimator's PRECISION, not the multiplier's magnitude; the note flags this as closing off 'a tempting but wrong inference' that Apple's concentrated index ownership implies a larger multiplier. Audited absence as verified: full-body keyword search of all three new sources (zero hits for 'Apple', 'AAPL', 'mega-cap' in KRY's 23,999-word body; no Apple breakdown in Easley et al.; no equity application in Banafti & Lee) plus a vault-wide search for Apple passive-ownership stakes / index weight returning zero results.
findings.recommendation: Add the KRY flow-vs-behaviour split so the 14 % figure carries a mechanism; add Bouchaud's monthly M~1 and the square-root law with Y~0.5 as the source of the sigma/volume prediction; add one sentence closing off the concentration-implies-larger-multiplier shortcut per Banafti & Lee; and replace the bare absence assertion with the searched-and-found-nothing statement.

findings.issue: The fair statement of the bull case for the rental strategy is argued entirely from the income statement and never cites the one market-priced test of it, which the interim note treats as real if low-authority Position-A evidence.
findings.evidence: interim-report-ai-late-follower-chosen-vs-revealed, Position A: 'the market explicitly rewarded this: Apple rose ~7% while hyperscalers lost ~$900B combined in a week over capex-ROI doubts' - Apple up ~7% around its January 2026 earnings while Amazon/Google/Microsoft lost roughly $900B in combined market cap in a week. The note labels the source (TradingKey) 'low-authority, cross-checked'. The same note carries Cook's fuller quote: 'We use a hybrid model... we use some third-party cloud and we do our own data centers... there are other locations on the P&L other than OPEX, like OCOGS, et cetera, that also have AI expenditures', and records that the Q3 FY2026 call contains zero mentions of 'Gemini' despite the January 2026 partnership.
findings.recommendation: Add the February 2026 divergence (Apple ~+7 % vs ~$900B combined hyperscaler market-cap loss in a week) to the bull case in 5.3 or 8.2 with the source-authority caveat, and extend the Cook quote to include the hybrid-model / OCOGS admission, which is what supports the draft's own claim that AI costs are not fully visible in the capex line. The zero-Gemini-mentions observation is a usable audited absence about disclosure quality.

findings.issue: The draft asserts the memory shock is the driver but gives only shipment-decline percentages. The magnitude of the input shock and the industry ASP move - the numbers that make the exogeneity claim quantitative - are omitted, as is the CIRP switcher-mix effect that cuts against the ASP thesis at the margin.
findings.evidence: interim-report-hardware-regime-and-required-services-cagr: IDC (Aug 26 2026, Popal/Jeronimo/Reith) documents a NAND/DRAM cost shock of +300%+ YoY pushing CY2026 global shipments down 16.7% (steepest ever) while smartphone ASP rises 27.6% to $581; 'IDC frames the mechanism explicitly as memory-input cost pass-through, not demand pull from AI features, and expects memory prices to stay elevated at least until 2028.' CIRP (Jul 2026): in the six months to March 2026 only 68% of Android switchers bought a current flagship versus 80% of upgrading legacy iPhone owners, switchers ~12% of iPhone buyers - 'a growing switcher cohort buys down the lineup'. The note also records Morgan Stanley cutting its PT to $360 on slower Services while raising its FY26 iPhone forecast to 243M units (+3.3%) - 'even the Services bear is not calling the iPhone cycle over'.
findings.recommendation: Add the +300 %+ YoY memory-cost shock and the industry ASP move (+27,6 % auf 581 $) so the exogenous-pass-through claim is quantified; add the CIRP switcher-mix datapoint (68 % vs 80 % flagship attach, switchers ~12 % of buyers) as a named second-order offset to the ASP thesis; and consider the Morgan Stanley PT-cut-while-raising-units pair in Section 8.3 as evidence that even the Services bear is not a hardware bear.
